headlines.summary: Workers are "time traveling" on LinkedIn to add AI skills to roles they left years ago, likely to get a leg up in a tough job market, researchers say.
headlines.article_text: Job seekers are adding AI skills on LinkedIn to roles they held pre-ChatGPT: researchers Skip Navigation Related Stories Work Use this 4-word phrase to stand out after a job interview: 'It can be really powerful,' says career coach Work Use the '10/10' rule to land a job: It's like tapping into 'the hidden job market,' says career coach Work Don't just follow your passion—'successful and happy' people prioritize 2 things in their careers, says expert Work The top 10 highest-paying jobs for teens in the U.S.—No. 1 isn't retail or food service Leadership Working overtime won't give you job security in the age of AI, say career experts: Stability is 'no longer a guarantee' Oscar Wong | Moment | Getty Images You've probably spruced up your resume for a job search before, maybe even added a few skills you didn't really have to seem like a stronger fit. In today's job market, some workers are "time traveling" on their LinkedIn profiles to add AI skills to jobs they left years ago, according to a working paper titled "Time Travel on Professional Profiles," published in July in the National Bureau of Economic Research. The researchers analyzed monthly captures of LinkedIn with help from workforce data company Revelio Labs. "It gives you a snapshot of what people think employers want," Nicholas Bloom, one of the paper's authors and the William D. Eberle Professor in Economics at Stanford University, tells CNBC Make It. The prevalence of AI-related terms, like LLM, GPT and artificial intelligence, spiked after late 2022 when OpenAI released ChatGPT, kicking off a wave of other generative AI chatbot launches. Nearly three-quarters of employers say AI skills are a strong advantage or even a requirement, according to a ZipRecruiter survey published in July. The number of occupational categories where job posts mention "AI" in the title has more than tripled in the U.S. since 2022, according to a report from Indeed also published that month. Job seekers might be thinking, "I know what employers are looking for, I know I need to hit on these buzzwords, so I go back and add them into my profile, even if they're not strictly true," Bloom says. Clarifying? Or lying? The research found that from 2020 to 2026, nearly 1 in 5 established U.S. LinkedIn users retroactively edited the title or description of a job they were no longer in. While the researchers can't definitively say why people made the changes, some of the edits are likely legitimate. If you weren't active on LinkedIn during your earliest jobs, for example, any modifications you make to those roles now amount to time traveling by default. The research picked up any difference of adding or subtracting at least one word in a job title or description, so changes like removing a duplicate word or adding an article like "the" also counted as time travel. Other changes might be less honest. The researchers noticed people adding AI skills to roles dating as far back as 2012, but it's "hard to believe" people might've used those skills in roles so far predating the AI boom, Bloom says. There's a chance they're exaggerating or outright fabricating information to get a leg up in the job search. The top offender by role was the self-professed AI product manager, with roughly 70% of these people making changes after leaving positions. "They claim to have been an AI product manager," Bloom says, but "it's hard to tell whether they really ever were." Some could've actually been product managers who discreetly slipped in "AI" a few years later to better their odds in the job market today, for example. The median time a person made a retroactive change was 4.5 years after they left the job, the researchers found. "It's kind of like the fashion cycle for job titles, job descriptions," Bloom says. Machine learning might've been the hot skill du jour a few years ago and cloud a few years before that. Today, as so many LinkedIn profile changes seem to reflect, it's AI. 'It's an arms race' The rate of this so-called time traveling on LinkedIn doubles shortly before people change jobs, the researchers found. Making these changes could be one way applicants are trying to cut through the noise in a tough market. The U.S. unexpectedly lost 23,000 jobs in July, and May and June's job numbers were revised downward by a cumulative 103,000. As AI makes it easier for candidates to quickly generate application materials, it also means they're up against more competition from other job seekers doing the same when vying for limited roles. On the other side of the table, many employers are hit with an influx of applications . To try to break through, job seekers may stuff keywords into their LinkedIn "just to get to the first round," Bloom says. "It's an arms race on both sides." Experts say whether you're actively looking for work or not, you should periodically update your professional work history, both on resumes and LinkedIn profiles. Aim to update once every three months and after every performance review, Jeff Hyman, CEO of Recruit Rockstars, told CNBC Make It in 2022. Add accomplishments, recognition or new responsibilities you might've received since your last update, with specific metrics to quantify — and make sure your resume and profile match . Having a full, detailed profile listing specific skills could help better surface you in recruiters' searches for candidates with certain qualifications. So when it comes to your LinkedIn profile, "more is almost always better than less," Bloom says, "as long as it's truthful." Want to get ahead at work? headlines.article_text: Apple announces new Mac Mini and Mac Studio models with AI upgrades Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Apple on Tuesday announced new Mac Mini and Mac Studio models with updated chips and other improvements for artificial intelligence applications. The announcement shows how desktop computers have become strategically important for Apple as a foothold in the AI development world and as a showcase for the AI capabilities of its chips. The Mac Mini can now be configured with two new chips, the M6 and M5 Pro, and now starts at $899, versus $799 for the prior model. In this article TSM AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The new Apple Mac Studio computer and Studio Display are displayed shortly after going on sale at the Apple Store on 5th Avenue in Manhattan, in New York City, New York, March 18, 2022. Mike Segar | Reuters With more consumers turning to Apple's computers for creating and running AI agents, the company is rolling out new Mac Mini and Mac Studio models with updated chips and other upgrades for artificial intelligence applications. The announcement, a few weeks before Apple is expected to release new iPhone models, shows how desktop computers have become strategically important for Apple as a foothold in the AI development world, and as a showcase for the capabilities of its processors. Developers using software like OpenClaw to create their own agents often prefer to run them on a dedicated Mac Mini computer instead of in the cloud. And Apple's Mac Studio is a popular choice for AI researchers who are experimenting with training and deploying local models. Apple highlighted in Tuesday's announcement that it builds its iPhone and Mac chips with special parts called neural engines dedicated to running models, and that it uses a RAM architecture that eliminates some memory bottlenecks. "With these frameworks and new chips, developers can run and fine-tune large AI models locally on their Mac," Apple said in the press release. The Mac Mini can now be configured with two new chips, the M6 and M5 Pro. It's the first Apple computer with an M6-generation chip, which is manufactured on a 2-nanometer process from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co . Read more CNBC tech news Marvell pops on AI chip deal that lets Google buy up to $12.2 billion in shares Nvidia plays matchmaker in Nordics, sources tell CNBC, as AI data center deals boom in region The U.S. banned Nvidia's best chips from going to China. Now it's trying to close a crucial loophole Amazon to expand drone service to nearly 500 cities after targeting 1 million deliveries this year The prior version was available with M4, M4 Pro and M4 Max chips. Apple said the computer configured with the M5 Pro can process large language model prompts 8.5 times faster than older Pro versions of the Mac Mini. Prices are also going up. The computer now starts at $899, up $100 from the prior model. That followed an increase over the summer from $599, which Apple blamed on memory costs. The Mac Studio is Apple's most powerful computer that doesn't have a built-in screen (Apple's Mac Pro was discontinued earlier this year). Some models will come with the M5 Max chip, which Apple says will allow LLMs to run nearly four times faster than its predecessor. Some can be configured with Apple's M5 Ultra chip, the most powerful chip Apple currently offers. And Apple says multiple Mac Studios with the Ultra chip can be linked together to work as one machine, pool memory together and run trillion-parameter frontier AI models. Mac Studio computers with an M5 Max chip start at $2,499 — the same as before — and a Mac Studio with the M5 Ultra starts at $5,499. Apple previously charged at least $5,299 for a Mac Studio with an Ultra chip, and the past model was equipped with an M3 Ultra chip, a generation behind. The new computers go on presale on Tuesday and will ship on Sept. 22.
